source.title_on_document: Large Language Model in Ideation for Product Innovation: An Exploratory Comparative Study

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplement or online appendix. Appendix A (mediation tables A1 to A5, pp. 33-37) is inside this PDF.

paper_design_summary: One hundred MTurk workers were randomly assigned to generate up to five new product ideas for coffee mugs using either a ChatGPT interface (GPT-3.5-turbo via the OpenAI API) or a Google Search interface (Custom Search JSON API) built into the task page. After removing ten who failed attention checks, 90 participants (45 per arm) remain. Valid ideas were summarized by ChatGPT, rated by MTurk workers for novelty and functional appropriateness, and scored for semantic divergence across ideas within each condition; idea counts and ideas per second were also compared.

studies.label: Online experiment: ChatGPT vs Google Search for coffee-mug ideation

assignment.what_was_assigned: Ideation tool embedded in the task interface: ChatGPT (LLM condition) or Google Search (Search Engine condition)
assignment.quote: Our study employs a between-subjects design consisting of two conditions: LLM and search engine. Participants were randomly assigned to one condition to generate innovative ideas for coffee mugs; each participant was allowed to submit up to five ideas.
assignment.locator: p. 9, Section 4 (Experimental Setup); also p. 11 and Table 1 randomization check, p. 12

arms.name: LLM
arms.description: Task page with a ChatGPT panel (OpenAI Chat Completion API, GPT-3.5-turbo) that kept recent conversation memory; participants could start a new conversation; at least one message required to reach the task page.

arms.name: Search Engine
arms.description: Task page with a Google Search panel (Google Custom Search JSON API); participants could browse result pages and open websites inside the panel; at least one query required to reach the task page.

participants.exclusions: 100 MTurk workers participated and were randomly assigned (p. 11); 10 who failed attention checks were removed, leaving 90 (45 per arm). Arm counts before exclusion are not given. Outcome-specific samples are smaller: 67 participants (39 LLM, 28 Search) submitted at least one valid idea and enter the novelty, functional appropriateness, and divergent thinking comparisons; productivity and efficiency use all 90 (Table 3, pp. 19-20).
participants.who: MTurk workers with more than 5,000 approved tasks and an approval rate of at least 99%; paid U.S.$1.50
participants.quote: Ten participants who failed attention checks were removed. Our final sample comprised 90 participants, with 45 for each tool.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT via OpenAI Chat Completion API, GPT-3.5-turbo
ai_tool.how_used: Free chat in a panel beside the idea-submission form; participants were told to use the assigned tool and not to use tools outside the interface. Ideas were typed by participants into five boxes (up to 500 characters each).

task.description: Come up with novel ideas for coffee mugs, up to five ideas, each up to 500 characters (Figure 2 screenshot, p. 10).

outcomes.name: Idea Novelty
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 300 MTurk raters (idea generators and attention-check failures excluded) each rated six random ideas on novel, original, exciting (7-point Likert); about 10.6 raters per idea; scores z-normalized within rater, averaged over the three items per idea, then averaged over each participant's valid ideas. Ideas were first summarized by ChatGPT (GPT-3.5-turbo) to at most 10 words and the summaries were what was scored. 228 valid ideas (159 LLM, 69 Search). Participants with no valid idea are missing. pp. 12-13, Section 5.1; p. 16, Section 5.2.3.

contrasts.reported: Idea Novelty: LLM 0.010 (39) vs Search Engine -0.057 (28); Difference 0.018 [as printed]; F-statistics 4.88** (one-way ANOVA). Text: 0.010 vs. -0.057, p < 0.05. No arm SDs printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 20, Table 3 Panel C; p. 19 text

outcomes.name: Functional Appropriateness
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same MTurk rating procedure as Idea Novelty, items useful, effective, feasible (7-point Likert), z-normalized within rater, averaged per idea and then per participant; scored on ChatGPT summaries of the ideas. p. 16, Section 5.2.3.

contrasts.reported: Functional Appropriateness: LLM 0.055 (39) vs Search Engine 0.213 (28); Difference -0.159; F-statistics 10.77*** (one-way ANOVA). Text: 0.055 vs. 0.213, p < 0.01. No arm SDs printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 20, Table 3 Panel C; p. 19 text

outcomes.name: Divergent Thinking (semantic divergence of ideas across participants)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: For each idea, 1 minus the average cosine similarity between its embedding and those of all other ideas from participants in the same condition; averaged over the participant's ideas. Embeddings from text-embedding-ada-002; footnote 10 reports TF-IDF embeddings give consistent results. Computed on ChatGPT summaries of the ideas. pp. 16-17, Section 5.2.3.

contrasts.reported: Divergent Thinking: LLM 0.134 (39) vs Search Engine 0.123 (28); Difference 0.011; F-statistics 25.68*** (one-way ANOVA). Text: 0.134 vs. 0.123, p < 0.01; higher = more diverse ideas. No arm SDs printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 20, Table 3 Panel C; p. 19 text

diversity_detail.metric: Per idea: 1 minus mean cosine similarity to all other ideas within the same condition; participant score = mean over that participant's ideas. Higher = more divergent (no sign reversal needed).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea against all other ideas from participants within the same condition (the wording does not say whether the participant's own other ideas are excluded)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: One-way ANOVA across participant-level scores (39 vs 28 participants)
diversity_detail.notes: Ideas were summarized by ChatGPT to at most 10 words before embedding. The text (p. 17) says participants who did not use the tools have missing values, but Table 3 n's (39, 28) match participants with at least one valid idea. Table 2 (p. 17) prints the Divergent Thinking row identical to the Functional Appropriateness row (Obs 67, mean -0.018, SD 0.126), which does not match the Table 3 arm means of 0.134 and 0.123.

outcomes.name: Productivity (number of valid ideas)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of valid ideas submitted (maximum five), after two postgraduate students removed invalid ideas (unrelated to mug design, duplicates, extra ideas in one box). p. 12, Section 5.1; p. 15, Section 5.2.3.

contrasts.reported: Productivity: LLM 3.533 (45) vs Search Engine 1.533 (45); Difference 2.000; F-statistics 27.65*** (one-way ANOVA). Text: 3.533 vs. 1.533, p < 0.01.
contrasts.locator: p. 20, Table 3 Panel C; p. 19 text

outcomes.name: Efficiency (valid ideas per second)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Ratio of the number of valid ideas to the time spent on the interface (seconds). A rate of idea production, not a creativity rating. p. 16, Section 5.2.3.

contrasts.reported: Efficiency: LLM 0.010 (45) vs Search Engine 0.003 (45); Difference 0.007; F-statistics 13.44*** (one-way ANOVA). Text: 0.010 vs. 0.003, p < 0.01.
contrasts.locator: p. 20, Table 3 Panel C; p. 19 text

company_involvement.description: Authors at HKUST and American University; no company funding or authorship stated. The study uses OpenAI and Google APIs as tools only.

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to ChatGPT or Google Search (an active non-generative comparison) for an idea-generation task (p. 9, p. 11). 90 people analyzed after 10 attention-check exclusions (p. 11); the rated creativity and diversity outcomes use 67 people (39 + 28) with at least one valid idea, still above 50. Novelty and appropriateness are rated by MTurk raters and divergence is computed from embeddings on the ideas (p. 16-17).

one_line_finding: ChatGPT users produced more valid ideas (3.533 vs 1.533, F = 27.65), more novel (0.010 vs -0.057, F = 4.88) and more divergent ideas (0.134 vs 0.123, F = 25.68), but less functionally appropriate ideas (0.055 vs 0.213, F = 10.77) than Google Search users (Table 3, pp. 19-20).
open_questions: Table 3 (p. 20) prints the Idea Novelty Difference as 0.018, while the printed arm means (0.010 and -0.057) differ by 0.067.

Table 2 (p. 17) looks internally inconsistent with Table 3: the 67-observation means printed for Idea Novelty (0.121) and Functional Appropriateness (-0.018) match the 39/28 weighted averages of the Table 3 Functional Appropriateness and Idea Novelty arm means respectively, which suggests the two rows are swapped in one of the tables; the Divergent Thinking row in Table 2 duplicates the Functional Appropriateness row. The text (p. 19) and Appendix Tables A3-A4 (positive ChatGPT coefficient on novelty, negative on appropriateness) agree with the Table 3 labels. Extraction should confirm with the authors.
No arm SDs are printed for any outcome; only arm means, n's, and ANOVA F-statistics. Table 2 gives pooled SDs (e.g., Idea Novelty 0.209, Productivity 2.057), but see the row-labeling issue above.
The creativity outcomes are scored on ChatGPT-generated summaries (at most 10 words) of participants' ideas, not on the original text (pp. 12-13).
Rated outcomes exclude participants without any valid idea (6 LLM, 17 Search), a post-randomization selection that differs by arm.
notes: Appendix A (pp. 33-37) reports mediation models where each outcome is regressed on a ChatGPT dummy plus one process variable, with coefficients, SEs, p-values and bias-corrected CIs; these ChatGPT coefficients are direct effects conditional on a mediator, not the total effect (e.g., Table A3, Idea Novelty on ChatGPT .0783577, SE .0328887, p 0.021, controlling for Information Adoption; Table A4, Functional Appropriateness on ChatGPT -.1665013, SE .0496893, p 0.002; Table A5, Divergent Thinking on ChatGPT .014556, SE .0023706, p 0.000). Observation counts for these models are not printed. Tables 4-5 (pp. 23-24) are adoption-novelty regressions on 49 participants and do not contrast the arms directly. Process variables (exploration breadth, information divergency, etc.) are not scored on participants' output and are not listed as outcomes.
